# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.

- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Recorded evidence

A 19×13 demonstration with background 4 changed only a two-cell horizontal component of color 1 at the top edge to color 0. A separate two-cell color-2 component remained unchanged, so size alone did not explain selection.

description: Use for ARC grid transformations; infer rules from demos.
---

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

See `references/continual-arc-instance-notes.md` for concise session-specific evidence and lessons from an ambiguous instance. # ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

See `references/continual-arc-instance-notes.md` for concise session-specific evidence and lessons from an ambiguous instance. # ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. - **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

name: arc-grid-reasoning
description: Use for ARC grid transformations; infer rules from demos.
---

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

See `references/continual-arc-instance-notes.md` for concise session-specific evidence and lessons from an ambiguous instance. # ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

I'm noticing that the color4 component involves a vertical line and a horizontal row, plus some other areas. For instance, there's a shape involving color6 that gets recolored to match color4, despite the target not matching the expected shape. The dimensions are different but share orientation. Additionally, there’s a transformation logic at play, where a duplicated shape potentially gets recolored based on specific rules about color or position. It's interesting how shapes may find their "mirror" in these patterns.

**Examining demo shapes**

In demo5, there are two L-shaped triominoes: one in color5 and the other in color6. It looks like color6 was chosen for replacement with color4, possibly because their colors were aligned. For demo7, there's potential for a repeated shape as well with two identical L components in color8. It's fascinating how the alignment and choice of colors influence which shapes are selected for replacement. I’m eager to see how these patterns play out!

**Analyzing object shapes**

I’m examining the objects in Demo3, Demo4, and Demo6 to see how they relate in terms of shape and color. It seems like Demo3's target might have a similar shape to component 0, while Demo4’s singleton seems to match another color. I need to check if Demo6's rectangles are the same size as others too. I need to find out how the duplicates are recolored based on their shapes and possibly replace one color with that of a third object.

**Evaluating puzzle rules**

I'm considering a puzzle where a set of multi-colored objects marks pairs with colors. Each object could act like an "arrow" pointing to another object as its destination. The test’s complex identical shapes of 6 and 4 suggest they were generated from the same template, but recolored differently based on the result. It seems that the demos show which among identically shaped objects is changing, highlighting pair shapes where one object is recolored according to a marker.

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. # ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

See `references/continual-arc-instance-notes.md` for concise session-specific evidence and lessons from an ambiguous instance. # ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

name: arc-grid-reasoning
description: Use for ARC grid transformations; infer rules from demos.
---

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.

- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

name: arc-grid-reasoning
description: Use for ARC grid transformations; infer rules from demos.
---

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. - **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level procedure for ARC and Continual-ARC tasks where demonstration pairs define an unknown grid transformation. Infer a compact, general rule rather than imitating one observed color change.

## Operating protocol

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record grid dimensions, background color, available demonstration count, wrong-attempt cap, and exact response/action format. In interactive streams, emit exactly one permitted action per turn and put the required machine-readable action on the final line.
2. **Represent the grid structurally.** Note the background, non-background colors, connected components, bounding boxes, pixel counts, repeated shapes, and boundary contact. Use 4-connectivity unless examples indicate diagonal connectivity. Keep separate components distinct even when they share a color.
3. **Compare every demonstration pixel by pixel.** Identify changed cells, group them into affected components, and distinguish recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or canvas edits. Record unchanged lookalikes as counterexamples that constrain the rule.
4. **Generate and test competing hypotheses.** Consider object properties (shape, size, position, edge contact, isolation), relationships (same size/shape, alignment, color pairing), and global patterns. A single example rarely proves a color mapping; validate against all demonstrations and untouched objects.
5. **Request demonstrations strategically.** If plausible hypotheses predict different outputs and another demo is available, request one rather than making a low-confidence guess. Balance the request cost against the cost of a wrong submission and remaining caps. Do not request reflexively after the rule is sufficiently constrained.
6. **Construct conservatively.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and change only cells licensed by the best-supported rule. Verify dimensions, row lengths, color range, and every changed coordinate before submitting.
7. **Use feedback diagnostically.** An incorrect submission rules out that proposed output, not necessarily all of the underlying analysis. Revisit transformed components and counterexamples; do not repeat a similar guess without new evidence.

## Common pitfalls

- **Overgeneralizing a one-example substitution.** In one stream instance, a two-cell color-1 component became color 0 in one demo, while a later demo changed a 16-cell color-0 component to color 6. A test guess that changed a color-7 trio to 0 was incorrect. Those examples do not establish a global color mapping; compare object identity and relationships as well as colors.
- **Ignoring unchanged counterexamples.** A component with the same color, size, or simple shape may remain untouched. Record it explicitly and ask what distinguishes the changed object.
- **Changing too much.** Preserve all input cells except those licensed by the inferred operation.
- **Treating more data as automatically better.** A demo has a cost; request it when it can separate live hypotheses, not merely because uncertainty exists.

## Further reading
